title: Adverbs and adverb placement
titleVi: Trạng từ và vị trí trạng từ
summary: Đặt trạng từ đúng chỗ — giữa trợ động từ và động từ chính, không chen giữa động từ và tân ngữ.
whyItMatters: Trạng từ sai vị trí là lỗi band 6 điển hình vì câu vẫn hiểu được nhưng nghe *lệch*: *I like very much this book*, *She speaks very well English*. Trong Writing Task 1, trạng từ chỉ mức độ (`sharply`, `steadily`, `marginally`) quyết định độ chính xác của mô tả xu hướng; đặt sai chỗ, câu mất tự nhiên và mất điểm Lexical Resource lẫn Grammar.

sections.heading: Adjective or adverb: what is being described?
body: An **adjective** describes a noun or pronoun: *a careful driver*, *the response was quick*. An **adverb** describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb: *she drives carefully*, *the response came quickly*, *remarkably cheap*.

The confusion starts with **linking verbs** — *be, seem, look, feel, sound, taste, become, remain*. After them you need an adjective, because the verb is describing the subject, not the action: *The plan looks risky* (not *looks riskily*).
So the same idea takes two shapes: *a **serious** problem* (adjective + noun) versus *the problem **seriously** affects rural schools* (adverb + verb).

examples.right: The number of cyclists rose sharply after the lane opened.
examples.wrong: The number of cyclists rose sharp after the lane opened.
examples.note: *Rose* is a verb, so it needs the adverb **sharply**.
**look** is a linking verb here → adjective.

sections.heading: Well, fast, late, hard — and the traps beside them
body: Some adverbs do not end in **-ly**: *fast*, *hard*, *late*, *early*, *well*. *Well* is the adverb of *good*: *She writes well*, not *She writes good*.
Three look-alike pairs cause most errors. **hard** = with effort; **hardly** = almost not. **late** = not on time; **lately** = recently. **near** = close; **nearly** = almost.
Notice how much the meaning shifts: *He works hard* (he is diligent) versus *He hardly works* (he does almost nothing). One letter changes the claim entirely.

rows: Rural teachers work hard for low pay.
The two groups hardly differ in income.
Lately, the city has focused on cycling.
Nearly half of respondents supported the tax.
The policy has worked well in small towns.

sections.heading: Mid position: before the main verb, after be
body: Adverbs of frequency and degree (**always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never, also, probably, definitely, hardly ever**) normally sit in **mid position**.

The pattern has three parts. Before a **main verb**: *We **usually** eat at home.* After **be**: *She is **always** late.* After the **first auxiliary**: *The meeting has **probably** finished.* If there are two auxiliaries, the adverb goes after the first: *The results will **definitely** be published.*
Mid-position adverbs never split a verb from its object. *I like very much this book* fails because *very much* sits between *like* and *this book*; write *I like this book very much*.

examples.right: The government has consistently underestimated demand for housing.
examples.wrong: The government has underestimated consistently demand for housing.

examples.right: We are usually charged for extra baggage.
examples.wrong: We usually are charged for extra baggage.

examples.right: She reads the report carefully every morning.
examples.wrong: She reads carefully the report every morning.
examples.note: Never put an adverb between verb and object.

sections.heading: End position: manner, place, time
body: When several adverbials end a sentence, the neutral order is **manner → place → time**: *She sang beautifully at the concert last night.*

This is a default, not a law. Putting **time** first gives it emphasis (*Last night she sang beautifully*), and putting **place** first is common when the place is the topic (*In rural areas, access remains limited*).

Keep long phrases out of the middle of the sentence. A short adverb can sit mid-sentence; a five-word prepositional phrase cannot: *The council, **in response to mounting criticism**, revised the plan* is fine, but *The council revised in response to mounting criticism the plan* is not.

examples.right: The proportion of graduates working abroad rose steadily between 2010 and 2020.
In coastal cities, property prices have doubled since 2015.
examples.note: Fronted place phrase for topic emphasis.

examples.right: She explained the method clearly at the start of the seminar.
examples.wrong: She explained clearly the method at the start of the seminar.

sections.heading: When position changes the meaning
body: Focus adverbs — **only, even, just, merely, particularly** — modify the word immediately after them. Moving them changes the claim: *Only the manager approved the budget* (nobody else) versus *The manager only approved the budget* (nothing more than approval).
Comment adverbs — **fortunately, surprisingly, frankly, arguably, theoretically** — usually open the sentence and evaluate the whole clause: *Surprisingly, the policy had little effect on prices.*
In academic writing, place hedges mid-sentence for a measured tone: *This **arguably** reflects a deeper skills mismatch*, rather than the blunt *This reflects a skills mismatch*.

examples.right: Only two of the ten regions met the target.
The region only met two of the ten targets.
examples.note: Different claim: it met two and no more.

examples.right: Arguably, the policy has done more harm than good.
examples.note: Comment adverb + comma frames the whole sentence as a judgement.

commonMistakes.why: Trạng từ không chen giữa động từ và tân ngữ. *English* là tân ngữ nên phải đứng ngay sau *speaks*.
**hardly** = hầu như không, nghĩa hoàn toàn khác **hard** = chăm chỉ. Đây là cặp dễ nhầm nhất vì *hardly* trông như trạng từ chuẩn của *hard*.

commonMistakes.wrong: The plan looks riskily to investors.
commonMistakes.right: The plan looks risky to investors.
commonMistakes.why: Sau động từ nối (**look, seem, feel, become**) dùng tính từ, không dùng trạng từ.

commonMistakes.wrong: The government has underestimated consistently the problem.
commonMistakes.right: The government has consistently underestimated the problem.
commonMistakes.why: Trạng từ tần suất đứng **sau trợ động từ đầu tiên** và trước động từ chính.

commonMistakes.wrong: Lately, he arrived late for the meeting.
commonMistakes.right: Recently, he arrived late for the meeting. / He arrived late for the meeting lately.
commonMistakes.why: **lately** = gần đây, không đồng nghĩa *late* = muộn. Ở đầu câu, *Lately* vẫn đúng ngữ pháp nhưng nghĩa là *gần đây*, không phải *muộn*.

ieltsTips: Trong Task 1, chọn trạng từ mức độ chính xác thay vì `very`: *rose **sharply** / **steadily** / **marginally***, *fell **modestly***, *remained **broadly** stable*. Mỗi trạng từ phải khớp với độ dốc thật của biểu đồ.
Đặt trạng từ tần suất vào giữa câu để câu Task 2 nghe học thuật: *Governments have **repeatedly** failed to address the shortage*, *Critics **often** argue that…*
Dùng comment adverb để mở câu nhận định, tạo giọng phê bình có kiểm soát: ***Arguably**, the benefits have been overstated.* ***Surprisingly**, fuel taxes provoked little opposition.*
Nhớ **only** đứng ngay trước từ nó giới hạn. Nếu muốn nói *chỉ có chính phủ*, viết *Only the government can…*; nếu muốn nói *chính phủ chỉ làm một việc*, viết *The government only…*.

exercises.question: The proportion of households renting privately rose ___ between 2005 and 2015.
The new measures look ___ on paper.
Which sentence is correct?
options: I like very much this policy.
I like this policy very much.
I very much like this policy much.
I like this very much policy.
exercises.explanation: The object stays next to the verb; *very much* goes at the end.

exercises.question: He ___ works; he spends most of the day on his phone.
exercises.explanation: The second clause shows he does almost nothing → **hardly**.

exercises.question: The committee has ___ reached a decision.
exercises.explanation: Positive statement with *has* → **already** (sooner than expected). *Yet* is for negatives and questions.

exercises.question: The team has ___ (probable) finished the fieldwork by now.
She explained the procedure ___ (clear) to the new staff.
___ (fortunate), the storm passed before the evacuation began.
exercises.explanation: A comment adverb opening the sentence → **Fortunately**.

exercises.question: The two cohorts ___ (hard / differ) in average income.
Only two regions ___ (meet) the target last year.
exercises.explanation: **only** limits the subject; the verb stays past simple **met**.
